title: Section 1202 Qualified Small Business Stock (C-corp owners)
summary: Tiered exclusion under OBBBA: 50% gain exclusion at 3-year hold, 75% at 4 years, 100% at 5 years. Per-issuer cap raised to $15M.
detailsHtml:
The mechanics — tiered structure under OBBBA (effective for stock issued after July 4, 2025)

If your business is structured as a C-corp from inception, your stock is acquired at original issuance, the company's gross assets are under $75M when issued, and the business meets the active-business and non-SSTB tests, you may exclude gain on sale according to a graduated schedule: 50% at 3 years held, 75% at 4 years, 100% at 5 years. Cap is the greater of $15M or 10× your basis, per issuer. State conformity varies sharply — California, for example, does not conform to §1202 at all, and the full federal gain remains taxable at the state level.

The 28% rate trap: The portion of gain NOT excluded under the partial 3- or 4-year regimes is taxed at 28%, not the standard 15% or 20% long-term capital gains rate. A 4-year exit on $20M of gain with the $15M cap excludes 75% × $15M = $11.25M; the remaining $8.75M is taxed at 28% plus 3.8% NIIT (~31.8%), materially worse than holding to 5 years for the full 100% exclusion.
OBBBA transition rules: The new tiered exclusion, $15M cap, and $75M gross-asset threshold apply only to stock issued AFTER July 4, 2025. Stock issued on or before that date remains under the old regime (5-year hold, $10M cap, $50M assets). Pre-OBBBA stock cannot be reorganized or exchanged into the new regime — §1202(i) prevents resets.
Founder example, post-OBBBA stock: Basis at company formation: $10,000 Sale price after 5 years: $20,000,000 Total gain: $19,990,000 Section 1202 exclusion (100% @ 5y): $15,000,000 Taxable gain (regular LTCG): $4,990,000 Federal tax (~23.8% w/ NIIT): ~$1,188,000 Same founder exiting at 4 years instead: Section 1202 exclusion (75% × $15M): $11,250,000 Taxable gain @ 28% + 3.8% NIIT: $8,740,000 × 31.8% = ~$2,779,000 Cost of early exit: ~$1.6M in additional federal tax

Who's excluded

The active business and SSTB rules remain unchanged. Specified Service Trades or Businesses — health, law, accounting, consulting, performing arts, financial services, athletics, brokerage, and businesses where the principal asset is the reputation or skill of employees — do not qualify for §1202 regardless of structure. Most successful service-business founders never get to use this. Product, technology, and manufacturing businesses are the typical beneficiaries.

Stacking the per-issuer cap across donees and trusts — pre-sale planning

§1202(g) gifting + non-grantor trust contribution can multiply the cap. The $15M per-issuer cap (or $10M for pre-OBBBA stock) applies per taxpayer. Gifts of QSBS to family members under §1202(g) — with holding-period tacking under §1223(2) — give each donee their own per-issuer cap, while contributions to non-grantor trusts (each a separate taxpayer) accomplish the same stacking with creditor-protected structure. A founder approaching a liquidity event with $60M of expected QSBS gain can pre-gift to a spouse and two adult-child non-grantor trusts to potentially stack 4× $15M = $60M of exclusion, vs. the $15M solo cap. This is a pre-sale lever — once the sale is signed, you cannot retroactively gift the stock and qualify. Coordinate with estate planning counsel; the holding-period tacking, beneficiary structure, and trust drafting all matter. Letter Ruling 9633004 sketches the holding-period mechanics on gifted QSBS.

§1045 60-day rollover — preserves the clock if you have to sell early

§1045 lets you avoid the 28% rate trap entirely by rolling. Sales of QSBS held more than 6 months but less than the 5-year hold can be rolled into replacement QSBS within 60 days under IRC §1045, preserving the original holding-period clock. The mechanics are tight (60-day window, the replacement must itself be QSBS-eligible at original issuance, basis tracking is complex), but the result is that an M&A exit before the 5-year hold doesn't force the partial-exclusion-plus-28%-rate path the §1202 §9.1 example above describes — it lets you redeploy into a follow-on QSBS-eligible issuer and continue accruing the 5-year clock. Commonly used in serial-founder situations.

AMT preference on excluded gain — §57(a)(7)

For pre-OBBBA QSBS at 50% or 75% exclusion, 7% of the excluded gain is an AMT preference item under §57(a)(7). For 100%-excluded stock (the standard 5-year hold under pre-OBBBA, and the new 5-year tier under OBBBA), the exclusion has generally been clean for AMT. The post-OBBBA 50%/75% tiers introduce uncertainty pending Treasury guidance on whether the §57(a)(7) preference attaches to the new partial-exclusion regimes. The conservative planning posture is to assume the preference still applies to the new early-tier exclusions until Treasury issues guidance to the contrary — particularly relevant for AMT-exposed taxpayers (state-tax-heavy jurisdictions, certain ISO-exercise profiles) where a $5M excluded gain at 7% preference + 28% AMT rate quietly produces ~$98K of additional tax that the headline §1202 framing didn't surface.
